title: Life Expectancy Analysis
text: Life expectancy varies significantly across countries and is closely linked to economic and educational factors. This analysis uses data from 2000 to 2015 provided by the World Health Organization (via Kaggle, 2019) to examine how Gross Domestic Product (GDP) and Schooling affect life expectancy across populations. A multiple linear regression model was applied to predict life expectancy based on a country’s economic output and average years of education. The results indicate a positive relationship between both predictors and life expectancy: countries with higher GDP and greater access to education tend to have higher average life expectancies. Conversely, nations with lower income levels and limited educational attainment consistently show reduced life expectancy.

title: Life Expectancy Model
text:
Life expectancy varies significantly across countries and is strongly influenced by economic and educational factors. This analysis uses data from 2000 to 2015, provided by the World Health Organization, to examine the relationship between life expectancy, Gross Domestic Product (GDP), and average years of schooling. A multiple linear regression model was fitted using GDP and schooling as predictors.
The results indicate that both GDP and schooling are statistically significant and positively associated with life expectancy (p < 0.001). Each additional year of schooling corresponds to a substantial increase in life expectancy, while higher GDP levels also contribute positively, though to a lesser extent. These findings highlight the crucial role of education and economic development in improving population health outcomes globally.

title: Regression Model
text:
We use the following multiple linear regression model:
\[
\text{LifeExpectancy}_{it} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \cdot \text{GDP}_{it} + \beta_2 \cdot \text{Schooling}_{it} + \varepsilon_{it}
\]

This table presents the results of a multiple linear regression model predicting Life Expectancy based on GDP and average years of schooling:

The Intercept (≈ 44.98) represents the estimated life expectancy when both GDP and schooling are zero.
The GDP coefficient (0.0001) suggests a small but statistically significant positive effect of GDP on life expectancy.
The Schooling coefficient (≈ 1.96) indicates that each additional year of schooling increases life expectancy by approximately 1.96 years.
The very low p-values (all < 0.001) for both predictors confirm that these relationships are highly statistically significant.

These results highlight the strong influence of economic and educational factors on public health outcomes.
